concepts.def: Amount of product formed at equilibrium
Conditions that boost yield often slow the rate
Cost of conditions (e.g. high pressure equipment)
Speeds up forward and backward equally — no yield change

walkthroughs.body_html:
Yield and rate often fight each other.

In the Haber, a very low temperature gives a great yield but a useless rate — you'd wait years for ammonia.

A very high pressure improves yield but costs huge amounts in strong equipment and energy to compress.

So engineers pick conditions that are 'good enough' on both — about 450 °C and 200 atm — and recycle unreacted N₂ and H₂.

A catalyst speeds up forward and backward reactions by the same factor.

So the equilibrium position doesn't change, and the yield is the same.

The benefit is reaching equilibrium faster — important commercially. Iron is used in the Haber; vanadium(V) oxide is used in the contact process.

Exam questions stack the changes. Take it step by step.

Example: in 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ (exo forward), if you increase temperature and remove SO₃ — which way does it shift?

Higher T pushes the endothermic way → backward. Removing SO₃ pushes forward to replace it. The two pull in opposite directions; the net shift depends on which change is bigger.

mcqs.q: Why does adding an iron catalyst to the Haber process NOT increase the yield of ammonia?
options: It only catalyses the backward reaction
It speeds up forward and backward reactions equally

mcqs.q: In the contact process 2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃ (exothermic), the BEST yield would come from...

numericals.q: An equilibrium with 5 moles of gas on the left and 3 on the right is compressed. By how many moles does the favoured (right) side differ from the unfavoured (left) side?
numericals.hint: Difference is left moles − right moles.

free_texts.q: If forward is exothermic, raising temperature shifts equilibrium which way: forward or backward?
free_texts.hint: Heat is absorbed by the endothermic direction — the reverse.
